item.title: Statistics: Hierarchical Models (Partial Pooling) — Daily Learning
item.description: Partial pooling estimates related groups together, borrowing strength across them instead of treating each group alone or lumping them all into one number. Take quarterbacks: a rookie who completed 16 of 20 passes for 80% should not automatically rank above a veteran at 68% on 400 passes, because the rookie's small sample gets pulled more toward the league average.

item.title: Big Idea: The Sorites Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: One grain of sand is not a heap, and adding a single grain to something that is not a heap cannot by itself turn it into one. In the Sorites paradox, running it in reverse from a heap of 1,000,000 grains, removing one grain cannot stop it being a heap, so repeated removal ends by calling even one grain a heap.

item.title: Statistics: Expected Value of Information — Daily Learning
item.description: Before you decide, new information is worth only as much as it improves the outcome you can expect. Take a $100 bet you put at 55% to win, with $190 back if it lands, for an expected value of about +$4.50: a $10 scouting report that would reveal the true win chance might be worth just $2 if it would change your bet only rarely, so do not pay $10 for $2 of value.

item.title: Big Idea: The Simulation Argument — Daily Learning
item.description: Nick Bostrom's argument, in "Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?", says at least one of three propositions must be true: humanity is very likely to go extinct before reaching a "posthuman" stage, any posthuman civilization is extremely unlikely to run a significant number of simulations of its evolutionary history, or we are almost certainly living in a computer simulation. The argument's…
item.content:encoded: Nick Bostrom's argument, in "Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?", says at least one of three propositions must be true: humanity is very likely to go extinct before reaching a "posthuman" stage, any posthuman civilization is extremely unlikely to run a significant number of simulations of its evolutionary history, or we are almost certainly living in a computer simulation. The argument's force is numerical: if a posthuman civilization ran a great many detailed simulations of its forebears, and those simulated minds were conscious, they would vastly outnumber the original minds.

item.title: Statistics: Calibration — Daily Learning
item.description: A forecast is calibrated, as a February 2026 explainer defines it, when its numbers tell the truth about themselves: call enough events 70%, and about 70% of them should happen. Say a model prices the Browns at a 30% chance to cover the spread across 100 bets, and they actually cover 48: badly miscalibrated, which is why being right on average matters more than being confident.

item.title: Big Idea: The Schelling Point — Daily Learning
item.description: Two strangers told to meet in New York with no contact tend to land on the same answer: noon at the information booth in Grand Central Terminal, the focal point Thomas Schelling named in The Strategy of Conflict (1960). It works because each person is simulating what the other will simulate, and shared culture hands them both a default answer they can trust.
